function: Multi-agent DQN selects common and private stream powers and codebook beam directions per slice in MISO RSMA; A2C agents above it split slice power and bandwidth (p. 9, 10).
system: Downlink MISO O-RAN: one BS with 128-element ULA, 100 single-antenna users in three slices, RSMA, hardware impairments; carrier not stated, 10 MHz; no RIS (p. 4, 5, 14).
method: Hierarchical multi-agent DRL: cooperative A2C-LSTM agents for inter-slice power and bandwidth, per-slice DQN agents for intra-slice power and beams; reinforcement learning with SLA-based rewards (p. 8, 12, 14).
data_channel: Own simulation: block-fading MISO channel, 4 paths, log-normal shadowing, path loss 120.9+37.6 log10(d) dB, Gauss-Markov fading; 240 m x 240 m area with synthetic traffic (p. 5, 6, 14).
test_conditions: Learning and evaluation in one simulated environment; sweeps of user speed (2 to 14 m/s), eMBB packet size and hardware impairment level; no unseen-condition test (p. 18, 19).
baselines: Random (RRA), greedy (GGA), equal (EEA) allocation; SA2C-T [7] (A2C inter-slice, ZF beams); SOTA scheduler with the same DRL structure but updates every step (p. 14, 15).
metrics: Utility (weighted spectral efficiency and SLA satisfaction ratio), spectral efficiency, per-slice SSR (QoS), training loss, training time in seconds (p. 7, 15, 16).
complexity: Measured training time only: about 6500 s versus 8600 s for SOTA; 6453 to 6962 s over impairment levels; no Big-O, FLOPs or inference time (p. 16, 19).
q1_support: p. 6: "more realistic conditions, we adopt a flat-and-block fading" - custom block-fading model (log-normal shadowing, path loss 120.9+37.6 log10(d) dB, 4 paths, Gauss-Markov fading); no 3GPP channel model and no measured data.
q2_support: p. 19: "Training time of proposed HiSO-CoMA framework under various levels" - Fig. 17 gives a training time per impairment level, which shows training per level; the speed, packet-size and impairment sweeps do not test a trained model on unseen conditions.
q3_support: p. 15: "SA2C-T scheduler [7]: This scheduler is one of the" most recent learned methods (A2C-LSTM, same authors), compared with random, greedy and equal allocation (RRA, GGA, EEA) on utility, spectral efficiency and SSR (Figs. 10 to 13).
q4_support: p. 16: "Figure 8 illustrates the training time of the proposed" framework against the SOTA scheduler; Figs. 8 and 17 give measured training time in seconds; no Big-O, FLOPs or inference time.
q5_support: p. 14: "All numerical experiments were conducted using Python" - own simulation with a custom channel and traffic model; no code or data link and no public dataset anywhere in the paper.
notes: Borderline at step 1: the inter-slice A2C level (slice power and bandwidth) is slicing, above the physical layer, but the intra-slice DQN level learns beam directions and stream powers for a 128-element ULA with RSMA, a physical-layer decision learned jointly with the slicing one, so item 4 does not exclude it; area 3 from the beam selection. Tables 1 to 3 and the figures are not in the extracted text, so I read them from the page images (pp. 5, 14, 16 to 19). The carrier frequency is not stated. q3 uses SA2C-T [7], an earlier A2C method of the same authors whose intra-slice beams use ZF; the SOTA scheduler shares the structure of the proposed method and is not counted. q4 rests on measured training time in seconds (Figs. 8 and 17) only. The reviewer should confirm the step 1, q3 and q4 calls.
